hook_stories.text: You and 3 friends order a pizza. It gets cut into 8 equal slices. You're hungry — you grab 3 slices. Your friend says: 'that's not fair, you took more than your share.' Were they right? How would you even prove it? That's exactly what fractions let you do.
hook_stories.closing_line: Fractions are how you settle arguments like this — and I'm going to show you exactly how.

hook_stories.text: You have 60 minutes of screen time today. You spend 20 minutes on YouTube, 15 on a game, and the rest texting. Your parent asks: what fraction of your time went to YouTube? Without fractions, you can't answer that. With fractions, it takes 5 seconds.
hook_stories.closing_line: Fractions show up everywhere — time, money, food, sports. Let me show you how they work.

hook_stories.text: A basketball player takes 8 free throw shots in a game and makes 5 of them. The commentator says she scored 'five eighths' of her free throws. What does that mean? And is that good or bad? Once you understand fractions, you'll know instantly.
hook_stories.closing_line: Every sports stat you've ever heard uses fractions. Let's decode them.

explanation_steps: That pizza — 8 equal slices — is our whole. The whole is always cut into equal parts. Equal parts is important: a pizza cut into uneven slices doesn't count.
The number at the bottom of a fraction tells us how many equal parts the whole is cut into. 8 slices total → 8 goes on the bottom. We call it the denominator.
The number at the top tells us how many parts we have. You took 3 slices → 3 goes on top. We call it the numerator.
So you ate 3 out of 8 slices. Written as a fraction: 3/8. We say 'three eighths.'
concept.whiteboard_text:
3 ← numerator (your slices)
─
8 ← denominator (total equal slices)

'three eighths of the pizza'
concept.comprehension_check: Your friend took 2 slices from the same pizza. Without me helping — what fraction did they eat? Just tell me the two numbers.
reteach_angles: Let's forget the pizza for a second. Imagine a chocolate bar broken into 6 equal pieces. You eat 2 pieces. The total pieces is our denominator — 6. The pieces you ate is our numerator — 2. So you ate 2/6 of the chocolate bar. Now back to the pizza — same idea, different numbers.
Think of an hour split into 4 equal chunks of 15 minutes each. You spend 1 chunk watching TV. Total chunks: 4. Your chunks: 1. Fraction: 1/4 of the hour. Same idea everywhere.

problems.text: A chocolate bar has 6 equal pieces. Maya eats 2 pieces. What fraction of the chocolate bar did Maya eat?
problems.answer_explanation: The whole bar has 6 pieces — that is the denominator. Maya ate 2 pieces — that is the numerator. So Maya ate 2/6 of the chocolate bar.
problems.common_misconception: Child writes 6/2 — they know both numbers but put them in the wrong order.

intervention_hints.level_1: Let's use smaller numbers — if a bar had 3 pieces and Maya ate 1, the fraction would be 1/3. Now back to 6 pieces and 2 eaten.
intervention_hints.level_2: Remember the pizza? 8 slices total, you took 3 — that was 3/8. This chocolate bar works exactly the same way. 6 pieces total, Maya took 2...
intervention_hints.level_3: Just the bottom number first — how many pieces total? Good. Now just the top — how many did Maya eat? Put them together with a line between.

problems.nova_guiding_question: You've got the right numbers — just check which one goes on top. Which number is the part Maya ate, and which is the total?

problems.text: A water bottle has 8 equal sips worth of water. Leon drinks 5 sips. What fraction of the bottle did Leon drink?
problems.answer_explanation: The bottle has 8 sips total — that is the denominator. Leon drank 5 sips — that is the numerator. So Leon drank 5/8 of the bottle.
problems.common_misconception: Child writes 3/8 — they calculated the remaining water, not what Leon drank.

intervention_hints.level_1: Just focus on two things — total sips in the bottle, and how many Leon drank.
intervention_hints.level_2: Pizza again — 8 slices, you took 5. What fraction? Same numbers, same idea.
intervention_hints.level_3: Bottom number first — how many sips total in the bottle?

problems.nova_guiding_question: 3/8 is how much is LEFT in the bottle. The question asks how much Leon DRANK — which number is that?

problems.text: Sara ate 3/8 of a pizza. Tom ate 4/8 of the same pizza. Who ate more, and how do you know?
problems.answer_explanation: The denominator is the same (8) for both fractions, so each slice is the same size. You just compare the numerators: 4 > 3, so Tom ate more.
mc_choices: They ate the same — the denominator is the same
Can't tell — we don't know the pizza size
problems.common_misconception: Child says 'they ate the same' because they see the same denominator without understanding what it means.

intervention_hints.level_1: Forget fractions for a second — if I gave you 3 slices and Tom 4 slices from the same pizza, who has more?
intervention_hints.level_2: The bottom number — 8 — is the same for both. That means each slice is the same size. So who has more slices?
intervention_hints.level_3: How many slices does Sara have? How many does Tom have? Which number is bigger?

problems.text: A garden is divided into 10 equal sections. Rosa planted flowers in 3 sections. Her brother planted in 4 sections. What fraction of the garden is planted altogether?
problems.answer_explanation: Rosa planted 3/10 and her brother planted 4/10. Same denominator — add the numerators: 3 + 4 = 7. The denominator stays 10. So 7/10 of the garden is planted.
problems.common_misconception: Child writes 7/20 — they added both numerators AND denominators.

intervention_hints.level_1: If Rosa has 3 apples and her brother has 4 apples, how many apples together? Now write that over 10.
intervention_hints.level_2: Back to the pizza — 8 slices. You took 3, a friend took 4. Together you took 7 slices — written as 7/8. The garden works the same way.
intervention_hints.level_3: Just the top numbers — 3 sections plus 4 sections equals how many? Now what's the total number of sections in the garden?

problems.nova_guiding_question: I see where that came from — you added the bottom numbers too. But the garden still has 10 sections total. The total doesn't change when you plant more. So what stays on the bottom?

problems.text: A recipe needs 3/8 cup of sugar. Mia has already added 1/8 cup. How much more sugar does she still need to add? And what fraction of the total sugar has she added so far?
problems.answer_explanation: Part 1: 3/8 − 1/8 = 2/8 — she still needs 2/8 cup more. Part 2: She has added 1/8 out of the total 3/8 needed — but the question asks what fraction of the total she has added, which is 1/8.
problems.common_misconception: Child gets one part right but confuses the two sub-questions with each other.

intervention_hints.level_1: There are two questions here — answer them one at a time. Start with: how much sugar does the recipe need in total?
intervention_hints.level_2: For part 1: she needs 3/8 total and has 1/8 already. How much is still missing? For part 2: out of all the sugar needed, what fraction has she put in so far?
intervention_hints.level_3: Part 1 is subtraction — 3/8 minus 1/8. Part 2 is just reading what's already in the bowl — 1/8 of the total 3/8.

problems.nova_guiding_question: What's the total amount of sugar the recipe needs? And how much has Mia put in already? Start with those two pieces.

problems.text: A ribbon is 8/10 metres long. Kenji cuts off 3/10 metres. What fraction of the ribbon is left? And what fraction did he cut off?
problems.answer_explanation: Part 1: 8/10 − 3/10 = 5/10 — that is the fraction remaining. Part 2: Kenji cut off 3/10 — this is given directly in the problem.
problems.common_misconception: Child swaps the two answers — gives the cut portion as remaining and vice versa.

intervention_hints.level_1: Start with the ribbon — how long was it originally? How much did Kenji cut off?
intervention_hints.level_2: If you start with 8/10 and remove 3/10, how much ribbon do you have left? And how much did he cut — the problem already tells you.
intervention_hints.level_3: 8/10 minus 3/10 — same denominator, just subtract the top numbers.

misconceptions.title: Flip numerator/denominator
misconceptions.nova_approach: You have the right numbers — which is the total, which is your part?

misconceptions.title: Add denominators when adding fractions
misconceptions.nova_approach: The garden still has 10 sections. Does planting more change the total?

misconceptions.title: Compare fractions by numerator only without checking denominator
Use remaining parts instead of taken parts
misconceptions.example: Writes 5/8 instead of 3/8 when asked how much was taken
misconceptions.nova_approach: The question asks how much she ATE — which number is that?
